thread.title: Subtracting Clarity Won't Make The Broadcom Case Stronger - Broadcom Limited (NASDAQ:AVGO)

author: Stephen Simpson, CFA
title: Subtracting Clarity Won't Make The Broadcom Case Stronger - Broadcom Limited (NASDAQ:AVGO)
text:
Operationally, I can’t really find much to criticize in Broadcom ’s ( AVGO ) fiscal fourth quarter, even if it does look like the wireless business is looking a little weaker heading into the next year. The central debate on Broadcom remains the CA acquisition and whether this foray into enterprise software can and will generate attractive returns for shareholders. The jury is still very much out on that, though management has made it clear that they look at this as a margin/FCF-rich opportunity and that they’re already willing to consider other enterprise software deals.
As I’ll discuss later, I think Broadcom’s move away from greater transparency is a mistake and disrespectful to shareholders, but it doesn’t really change the intrinsic value. Between a chillier market for semiconductor stocks and ongoing concerns about the CA deal, Broadcom continues to look undervalued below $300.
Choppy Top-Line Results, But Strong Margins In the last quarter before the inclusion of the CA deal, Broadcom had mixed but generally positive results. Revenue rose about 12% from the prior year (and more than 7% from the prior quarter), which was good for a small beat relative to sell-side expectations. Margin performance was more impressive, though, and drove a good 5% beat at the operating line.
Breaking down the revenue results, the Wired business was up 3% (missing by almost 4%) on persistent weakness in the broadband business as carriers delay/push out new programs. A very health datacenter business (up 22% yoy) helped offset this, though. The Wireless business saw a 5% yoy decline in revenue, but a 32% qoq rebound driven by the Apple ( AAPL ) iPhone launch, and this result was about 4% better than expected. Storage (up 96% yoy/up 1% qoq) was more than 2% ahead of expectations, with good results in the organic storage business, while the tiny Industrial/Other business was up 6% yoy and 21% qoq.
Helped in large part by a better mix (stronger datacenter, weaker broadband), gross margin rose five points from the year-ago level and more than a point from the prior quarter, beating expectations by almost a point and a half. Operating expenses were well-controlled, rising 11% yoy and falling 1% sequentially, coming in a little lower than expected and driving 25% operating income growth (up 13% qoq) and about five points of non-GAAP operating margin expansion.
Some Challenges In Semis, But Also Some Opportunities The incorporation of CA (and the changes in that business from the recent sale of Veracode and Broadcom’s cost-cutting plans) does contemplate guidance some, but it looks like the core semiconductor business is a little weaker than expected heading into fiscal 2019, and the guidance looks more backend-loaded than you’d like to see.
A weaker outlook for the semiconductor business is really not so surprising. While the newest Tomahawk and Jericho products will certainly help, and the broadband business should recover, weaker than expected volumes for the new iPhones have reverberated through the Apple supply chain, and peers/rivals like Qorvo ( QRVO ) have likewise lowered expectations as a result.
Although the weaker volumes for Apple are disappointing, the Wireless business at Broadcom arguably gets more attention than it really should. It’s still a big business, but Broadcom generates almost as much revenue from datacenter customers, and I continue to believe that investors underestimate the future contributions of businesses like custom ASICs for datacenters – a business that could generate more than $1 billion in revenue just with Google in 2020.
Big Plans For CA If it wasn’t clear before, it is clear now that Broadcom management is looking to strip virtually every possible cost out of CA and run it as a high-margin legacy cash cow type of business. In addition to selling Veracode to Thoma Bravo, there have already been reports of substantial firings at CA (around 40% of the employee base) and management said they’re restructuring the business to focus on high-margin revenue generation from its 500 current customers.
Broadcom is frankly not interested in investing in growth here – it’s not looking to expand sales channels or develop new products. Although I think the latter could be a mistake (developing new products can/could help extend the long-term usefulness of mainframes for established customers), it may make more sense long term to let others do the development work and then acquire them, and Broadcom management made it clear that they’re open to further enterprise software acquisitions in the future.
Soapbox Time This is the part of the article where I’m going to shake my cane and rant a bit, so readers who aren’t interested in that should skip to the Outlook section.
Although Broadcom has done well for investors over the long term and announced a substantial increase in the dividend with fiscal fourth quarter earnings, management is taking some steps I regard as shareholder-unfriendly by ending quarterly guidance and moving to a very vague reporting structure.
To be honest, I don’t care much about the quarterly guidance – I believe Wall Street is too focused on the short term as is. But I believe this is a bad move today, as Broadcom’s sell-side coverage base is made up of semiconductor analysts who are not very familiar with software business models. In dropping quarterly guidance, I believe Broadcom is setting the stage for volatile stock price action around the quarterly reports as analysts work to “dial in” the new moving parts of the business.
Moving to a reporting structure (Infrastructure Software and Semiconductor Solutions) that will no longer break out the results of Wired, Wireless, Storage, and so on is not okay in my book. Investors are co-owners of the business and they have a right to that information; virtually all pharmaceutical companies report the sales of individual drugs and many companies across a range of industries report segment-level revenue and operating profit detail (and some include gross margin and other details), and I see no reason why Broadcom cannot. I won’t sell Broadcom just because of this, but I hope other investors (particularly institutional investors) will push back hard on this and at least get them to commit to more detail in the quarterly regulatory filings.
The Outlook I continue to believe that Broadcom will generate mid-single-digit revenue growth over the long term, with a FCF growth rate about 2% higher as the company strips costs out of the CA business and continues to leverage strong share in many core markets into rich margins. Both discounted free cash flow and margin-driven EV/revenue lead me to fair values in the range of $290 to $295. Additional M&A seems quite likely, though it remains to be seen if Broadcom will make any further attempts in the future to acquire semiconductor businesses.
The Bottom Line Broadcom’s shareholder-unfriendly reporting changes don’t make the investment case stronger, but I believe the underlying business is still in good shape and undervalued by the Street. While iPhone volumes are a near-term threat, I believe they’re largely in the stock price now and I believe longer-term datacenter opportunities still have enough underappreciated upside to make these shares worth owning.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AVGO.
